metadata.summary: These European clinical practice recommendations address primary pediatric low-grade gliomas across tumor locations, ages, predisposition syndromes and selected clinical circumstances. They cover diagnostic evaluation, histopathology and molecular pathology, indications for treatment, and multidisciplinary decisions about initial surgery and nonsurgical therapy. They also discuss adverse effects, clinical assessments and follow-up, with attention to preserving neurological, visual, endocrine and functional outcomes.

target_population: Children and adolescents with low-grade gliomas

toxicities.dose_modifications: If a change is needed to complete first-line treatment, the alternatives given are cisplatin/vincristine (A) with cyclophosphamide/ vincristine (B) every 6 weeks [LGG2004 protocol], or a switch to weekly vinblastine monotherapy. No severity-based criteria are provided.

toxicities.incidence: In the published series using 6 mg/m2, almost 70 % of patients required a reduced dose because of hematological toxicity.
toxicities.dose_modifications: The published series used 6 mg/m2, with dose reduction required in almost 70 % of patients. A proposed starting dose, not tested in protocols with published data, is 0, 17 mg/kg BW or 5 mg/m2 (max:10 mg/dose) iv push weekly for BSA<0,6 m2 or BSA≥0.6 m2, respectively. No toxicity-grade thresholds for reduction are given.

prevention: Radiotherapy is especially deferred in younger patients. Selection of radiotherapy should account for age, tumour site and radiation exposure to the left temporal lobe and left hippocampus. Modern high-precision techniques, including proton therapy, may limit long-term toxicity.
Radiotherapy is especially deferred in younger patients and should be avoided as much as possible in children with NF1. A dose under 54 Gy could reduce the risk of vasculopathy.
Radiotherapy is especially deferred in younger patients to limit late effects. Its potential effects depend in part on exposure of the hypothalamic-pituitary region.
Radiotherapy is especially deferred in younger patients to limit late effects.
Radiotherapy should be avoided as much as possible in children with NF1 because their risk of a second malignancy is increased. Delaying or avoiding radiotherapy is an aim of chemotherapy in pLGG.

toxicities.event: Postoperative cerebellar and cranial nerve complications
prevention: For posterior fossa tumours, the multidisciplinary team should weigh these risks when considering gross total resection. Surgery in high-risk brain regions should be performed only by paediatric neurosurgeons experienced in those regions.

therapies_index.name: Carboplatin-Vincristine regimen
approved_indications: First-line systemic treatment for pLGG requiring non-surgical therapy.
therapies_index.administration: The European schedule lasts 81 weeks and comprises induction followed by consolidation.
key_toxicities: Hypersensitivity reactions to carboplatin become more frequent with repeated exposure; reported rates are between 6 % and 32 %.
monitoring: Blood count including neutrophils before each course.
GFR* and audiometry every 6 months during a platinum-based regimen.
Brain MRI, with spinal MRI when applicable, at week 24,54 and 84 or every 3–6 months until treatment ends according to institutional policy.

therapies_index.name: carboplatin
approved_indications: Component of the standard first-line systemic regimen for pLGG.
key_toxicities: Hypersensitivity reactions increase with repeated exposure to carboplatin; reported rates range between 6 % and 32 %.
monitoring: Watch for hypersensitivity during repeated exposure.
GFR* and audiometry every 6 months during a platinum-based regimen.

therapies_index.name: vincristine
approved_indications: Component of the first-line carboplatin and vincristine regimen for pLGG.
Component of the alternative cisplatin/vincristine (A) and cyclophosphamide/ vincristine (B) schedule following carboplatin hypersensitivity.

therapies_index.name: cisplatin/vincristine (A) with cyclophosphamide/ vincristine (B)
approved_indications: An alternative for completing first-line pLGG treatment after carboplatin hypersensitivity.
therapies_index.administration: The (A) and (B) combinations are given every 6 weeks according to the LGG2004 protocol.
monitoring: GFR* and audiometry every 6 months during a platinum-based regimen.
Audiometry and renal-function follow-up after chemotherapy as described for patients exposed to Carbo/Cisplatin or platinum-based chemotherapy.

therapies_index.name: cisplatin
approved_indications: Component of the alternative first-line completion schedule after carboplatin hypersensitivity.
monitoring: GFR* and audiometry every 6 months during a platinum-based regimen.
Audiometry and renal-function follow-up after platinum-based treatment.

therapies_index.name: cyclophosphamide
approved_indications: Component of the alternative first-line completion schedule after carboplatin hypersensitivity.

therapies_index.name: Vinblastine regimen
approved_indications: First-line treatment for pLGG requiring chemotherapy.
An alternative for completing first-line treatment after carboplatin hypersensitivity.
therapies_index.administration: Weekly monotherapy is continued to a total treatment duration of 70 weeks. The proposed starting dose, which has not been tested in protocols with published data, is 0, 17 mg/kg BW iv push weekly for BSA<0,6 m2 or 5 mg/m2 (max:10 mg/dose) iv push weekly for BSA≥0.6 m2. Published series used 6 mg/m2.
key_toxicities: Hematological toxicity required dose reduction in almost 70 % of patients receiving the 6 mg/m2 dose in published series.
monitoring: Blood count including neutrophils before each course.

therapies_index.name: vinblastine
approved_indications: First-line monotherapy for pLGG requiring chemotherapy.
Alternative treatment after carboplatin hypersensitivity.
therapies_index.administration: The proposed, not protocol-tested, starting dose is 0, 17 mg/kg BW or 5 mg/m2 (max:10 mg/dose) iv push weekly for BSA<0,6 m2 or BSA≥0.6 m2, respectively. Published series used 6 mg/m2.
key_toxicities: Hematological toxicity prompted dose reduction in almost 70 % of patients in published series using 6 mg/m2.
monitoring: Blood count including neutrophils before each course.

therapies_index.name: dabrafenib plus trametinib
approved_indications: FDA- and EMA-approved first-line treatment for pediatric patients ≥1 year of age with low-grade glioma harboring a BRAF V600E mutation who require systemic therapy.

therapies_index.name: dabrafenib
approved_indications: Used with trametinib as an approved first-line combination for pediatric patients ≥1 year of age with low-grade glioma harboring a BRAF V600E mutation who require systemic therapy.

therapies_index.name: trametinib
therapies_index.mechanism: The document identifies trametinib as a MEK inhibitor.
approved_indications: Used with dabrafenib as an approved first-line combination for pediatric patients ≥1 year of age with low-grade glioma harboring a BRAF V600E mutation who require systemic therapy.

therapies_index.name: selumetinib
therapies_index.mechanism: The document identifies selumetinib as a MEK inhibitor.

therapies_index.name: tovorafenib
therapies_index.mechanism: The document identifies tovorafenib as a type II RAF inhibitor.
approved_indications: FDA-approved for LGG with a RAF alteration that relapses after first-line therapy.

therapies_index.name: Everolimus
approved_indications: Medical treatment considered for SEGA after a multidisciplinary decision on medical versus surgical therapy.
therapies_index.administration: For patients with SEGA and TSC, 7 mg/m2 BSA po once daily at age ≥1 year and < 3 years, or 4.5 mg.m2 BSA po once daily for patients> 3 years; the target trough level is 5–15 ng/ml.
monitoring: Trough levels, targeting 5–15 ng/ml.

therapies_index.name: mTOR inhibitor
approved_indications: Indicated for SEGA(s) requiring intervention when the tumour cannot be operated on, surgery is contraindicated, surgery cannot achieve complete resection, or bilateral fornix lesions are present.

therapies_index.name: surgical resection
approved_indications: The principal treatment approach for LGG when resection is feasible.
therapies_index.administration: The surgical approach depends on tumour location, imaging-defined boundaries, histology, expected benefit and risk to neurological function.
key_toxicities: Resection in eloquent regions can cause permanent neurological deficits.
Posterior fossa surgery can be followed by cerebellar mutism syndrome, cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome or cranial nerve dysfunction.
monitoring: Postoperative MRI within 24–72 h to assess residual tumour unless suitable intra-operative or immediate postoperative MRI is available.
Neurological function after treatment.

therapies_index.name: Gross total resection
approved_indications: Initial therapeutic approach when complete removal is feasible.
therapies_index.administration: For posterior fossa tumours, the potential neurological consequences should be addressed by the multidisciplinary tumour board.
key_toxicities: Posterior fossa resection carries risks including cerebellar mutism syndrome, cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome and cranial nerve dysfunction.
monitoring: Postoperative MRI within 24–72 h unless suitable intra-operative or immediate postoperative MRI is available.
Ongoing surveillance; less frequent imaging after the 5th year can be considered following gross total resection.

therapies_index.name: partial resection
approved_indications: An approach often more appropriate than complete resection for tumours of the supratentorial midline, optic pathway/hypothalamus or brainstem.
Removal of accessible exophytic portions of optic pathway or chiasmatic hypothalamic tumours may improve tumour control.
monitoring: Postoperative MRI to evaluate residual tumour.

therapies_index.name: biopsy
approved_indications: Should be carefully considered for symptomatic tumours when an experienced paediatric neurosurgeon does not recommend resection, except for NF1-related OPG.
Can be considered for NF1-LGG outside the optic pathway, particularly with progression or atypical imaging, when feasible.
therapies_index.administration: Available approaches include neuroendoscopy, stereotactic biopsy and robot-assisted biopsy. Typical intrinsic optic pathway tumours associated with NF1 generally do not need biopsy at diagnosis unless trial-related biological assessment or atypical features warrant it.

therapies_index.name: neuroendoscopy
approved_indications: An option for tumour biopsy.
A minimally invasive option for evolving tumour cysts or disturbances of CSF circulation at diagnosis or during long-term follow-up.
therapies_index.administration: May be used together with neuronavigation.

therapies_index.name: stereotactic or robot-assisted biopsies
approved_indications: Surgical biopsy options that can yield the information needed for molecular assessment.

therapies_index.name: endoscopic third ventriculostomy
approved_indications: CSF diversion often achievable by this approach for tectal plate gliomas presenting with raised intracranial pressure.

therapies_index.name: CSF diversion
approved_indications: Usually needed at diagnosis for symptomatic tectal plate gliomas.
therapies_index.administration: Can often be achieved by endoscopic third ventriculostomy.

therapies_index.name: shunt technology
approved_indications: A minimally invasive surgical option to consider for disturbances of CSF circulation at diagnosis or during long-term follow-up.
monitoring: Audiometry during follow-up is described for patients with a CSF shunt.

therapies_index.name: microsurgery
approved_indications: A surgical technique used in paediatric neuro-oncological operations.

therapies_index.name: neuronavigation
approved_indications: An operative tool for paediatric neuro-oncological surgery and an adjunct to neuroendoscopy.

therapies_index.name: intraoperative imaging (iUS or iMRI)
approved_indications: An operative aid in paediatric neuro-oncological surgery.

therapies_index.name: intraoperative neuromonitoring
approved_indications: An operative aid in paediatric neuro-oncological surgery; required when resection of an infiltrative spinal pLGG is indicated.

therapies_index.name: radiotherapy
approved_indications: A standard salvage treatment for pLGG.
A possible primary treatment in selected cases when surrounding normal tissue can be optimally spared.
Up-front treatment may be considered after multidisciplinary agreement if minimal tumour growth threatens substantial morbidity or the risk of radiotherapy-related neurocognitive effects is low.
therapies_index.administration: The recommended dose is between 50.4 and 54 Gy. Treatment is especially delayed in young patients and should be avoided as much as possible in children with NF1.
key_toxicities: Potential long-term neurocognitive, neurological, endocrine and vascular effects.
Children with NF1 have increased risks of second malignancy and late vascular effects.
Radiation-related vasculopathies, including moya-moya, are a particular concern in younger patients.
monitoring: Long-term neurological, neurocognitive, endocrine and vascular effects.
Audiometry according to age and dose to the acoustic system, with regular assessment when hearing is impaired or the acoustic nerve lies within the RT field.
Endocrine assessment at completion and one year after radiotherapy, followed by assessments according to growth status and exposure of the pituitary hypothalamic region.

therapies_index.name: conformal radiotherapy
key_toxicities: Patients younger than 5 years of age appear to have the greatest risk of sequelae, including moya-moya and cognitive decline; deficits in supratentorial midline locations can increase over time.

therapies_index.name: proton therapy
approved_indications: A modern high-precision radiotherapy technique with the potential to limit long-term toxicity.
key_toxicities: Neurocognitive decline has been observed in children with LGG younger than 7 years old when tumour location results in greater volume and/or dose to the left temporal lobe or hippocampus, even with proton therapy.

therapies_index.name: craniospinal irradiation
approved_indications: May be an option for children with disseminated disease when chemotherapy has failed.

therapies_index.name: thyroid hormone
approved_indications: Hormone substitution on which children with CHG may depend.
therapies_index.administration: Hormonal treatment may continue without adjustment during chemotherapy.

therapies_index.name: hydrocortisone
approved_indications: Hormone substitution on which children with CHG may depend.
therapies_index.administration: Hormonal treatment may continue without adjustment during chemotherapy.

therapies_index.name: growth hormone
approved_indications: Hormone substitution on which children with CHG may depend.
therapies_index.administration: Hormonal treatment may continue during chemotherapy, but decisions about discontinuing growth hormone substitution follow institutional guidance because conclusive evidence is lacking.

therapies_index.name: anti-diuretic hormone
approved_indications: Hormone substitution on which children with CHG may depend.
therapies_index.administration: Hormonal treatment may continue without adjustment during chemotherapy.

therapies_index.name: epilepsy medication
approved_indications: Treatment of epilepsy when indicated in patients with pLGG.
therapies_index.administration: Generally continued when indicated during tumour treatment.
monitoring: Check possible interactions involving anti-epileptic drugs.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients whose tumour can be removed without an unacceptable risk of lasting functional harm.
decision_rules: Assess anatomical location, imaging-defined margins, histology and potential neurological harm when deciding whether to operate.
Use gross total resection as the initial treatment when feasible; discuss the expected benefit and surgical risks in a multidisciplinary tumour board.

recommended_regimens.name: Gross total resection
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred initial surgical approach when the tumour can be safely removed. The cited CCG9891/POG9130 study reported outcomes for children with confirmed gross total resection.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: CCG9891/POG9130: 5-year PFS of 94 % and OS of 99 % in children with confirmed gross total resection.

response_assessment.method: Postoperative MRI, unless a suitable intra-operative or immediate postoperative MRI is available.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine the amount of residual tumour.

response_assessment.timepoint: Approximately 2–3 weeks after surgery, when indicated
response_assessment.method: Repeat MRI if extensive postoperative parenchymal changes obscure residual tumour and treatment is urgently needed.
response_assessment.interpretation: Better delineation of residual disease may inform treatment.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The multidisciplinary decision should account for long-term neurological, visual, endocrine and functional outcomes. For posterior fossa tumours, address the risks of cerebellar mutism syndrome, cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome and cranial nerve dysfunction.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with tumours in surgically high-risk locations, including the supratentorial midline, optic pathway/hypothalamus or brainstem, or with symptomatic tumours for which an experienced paediatric neurosurgeon does not recommend resection.
decision_rules: Consider partial resection or biopsy rather than complete removal when the tumour occupies an eloquent region.
If resection is not advised, thoroughly consider biopsy for a symptomatic tumour, except for NF1-related OPG.
Have a multidisciplinary tumour board weigh surgical risk against therapeutic benefit and the value of histological and molecular diagnosis.
Only paediatric neurosurgeons experienced in the relevant high-risk region should undertake biopsy or resection there.

recommended_regimens.name: Partial resection
recommended_regimens.summary: Often a more appropriate surgical approach than complete removal in eloquent locations; accessible exophytic portions of chiasmatic hypothalamic gliomas may be removed in part to improve tumour control.

recommended_regimens.name: Biopsy
recommended_regimens.summary: An option for obtaining histological and molecular information when safe resection is unsuitable. Described approaches include neuroendoscopy, stereotactic biopsy and robot-assisted biopsy.

response_assessment.method: Diagnostic or prebiopsy MRI when surgery is not indicated or only a small biopsy is obtained.
response_assessment.interpretation: May serve as the pretreatment baseline.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In eloquent areas, intraoperative MRI or monitoring may be appropriate, and a second surgical opinion or discussion may be relevant.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients managed without immediate additional treatment after surgery, including those without residual tumour or with stable residual disease.
decision_rules: Use clinical and imaging surveillance when treatment is not indicated.
Base follow-up on age, NF1 status, tumour site, extent of resection, integrated pathological diagnosis, treatment history and time since diagnosis.
After the 5th year, less frequent imaging than the proposed follow-up schedule may be considered following gross total resection.

recommended_regimens.name: Observation
recommended_regimens.summary: Surveillance is a management pathway for patients without an indication for active treatment, including those with stable postoperative residual tumour.

response_assessment.method: Physical and neurologic examination and auxology every 3 months; every 3–6 months; every 6 months; and annually, respectively.
response_assessment.interpretation: Clinical surveillance for changes requiring reassessment of management.

response_assessment.method: Cranial and/or spinal MRI every 3–6 months; every 3–6 months; every 6–12 months; and annually, respectively.
Ophthalmology every 3 months; every 3–6 months; every 6 (-12) months; and every 6–12 months, respectively, when indicated; assessment is mandatory for OPG.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Neurocognitive assessment follows institutional policy. Late relapse can occur, although it is rare.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with unresectable LGG who need non-surgical treatment because of progression, neurological or visual findings, or other specified treatment indications.
decision_rules: Radiological indications include tumour-volume increase of > 25 % under RAPNO criteria, involvement of a previously unaffected area, a new lesion, or an increase in the number and/or size of metastases; report optic-nerve diameter increase separately.

Neurological indications include diencephalic syndrome, focal deficits or increased intracranial pressure attributable to tumour growth, drug-resistant seizures with or without growth, and symptomatic metastases.

Visual indications include definite loss, borderline vision or a threat to vision, deterioration of remaining low-level vision or visual field, nystagmus caused by visual impairment in infants, any loss in the second eye when the first is blind, or deterioration on follow-up. Significant visual loss is defined as more than or equal to 0.2 LogMAR.
Discuss treatment and follow-up using multidisciplinary clinical, imaging and functional information.

recommended_regimens.name: Carboplatin-Vincristine
recommended_regimens.summary: The most commonly used first-line systemic regimen; the European schedule has induction followed by consolidation.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the SIOP LGG 2004 Trial, 5-year OS was 89 % and PFS was 46.1 %. A different carboplatin and vincristine schedule and dosage evaluated by the Children’s Oncology Group yielded 39 % event-free survival (EFS) for non-NF1 patients.

recommended_regimens.name: Vinblastine
recommended_regimens.summary: First-line monotherapy used in several centres, initially for NF1 and older patients. The published-series dose was 6 mg/m2; almost 70 % of patients needed a reduction because of haematological toxicity. A proposed, but not tested in protocols with published data, weekly starting dose is 0, 17 mg/kg BW for BSA<0,6 m2 or 5 mg/m2 (max:10 mg/dose) for BSA≥0.6 m2, given iv push.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The Canadian group reported 5-year PFS of 42 % in non-NF1 patients.

response_assessment.timepoint: At diagnosis; at week 24,54 and 84, or every 3–6 months until end of therapy according to institutional policy; at end of therapy
response_assessment.method: Brain MRI, with spinal MRI when indicated.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess tumour status against baseline; consider MRI at week 12 in infants and patients with visual threat.

response_assessment.timepoint: At baseline; every three months during treatment; at end of therapy
response_assessment.interpretation: Classify neurological function as stable, worse or improved relative to baseline.

response_assessment.timepoint: At baseline; every 3 months during treatment for optic-pathway involvement, or earlier if clinically indicated; at end of therapy
response_assessment.method: Age-appropriate visual acuity and visual-field assessment, supported by fundoscopy and OCT.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine whether vision is stable, worse or improved relative to baseline.

supportive_care: Obtain blood counts, including neutrophils, and the specified biochemical assessments before each course and at the end of therapy.
For platinum-based treatment, the proposed assessments include GFR* every 6 months and audiometry in selected cases every 6 months.

Continue indicated hormonal replacement during chemotherapy without adjustment; decisions about stopping growth hormone replacement follow institutional guidelines because conclusive evidence is lacking.
Continue indicated epilepsy medication while checking for interactions with chemotherapy; check supportive-care medication interactions as well.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Course definitions vary by regimen. The clinical goal includes preservation of neurological, visual, endocrine and functional outcomes.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients receiving first-line Carboplatin-Vincristine who develop carboplatin hypersensitivity.
decision_rules: Be alert for carboplatin hypersensitivity, which becomes more frequent with repeated exposure; the reported range is 6 % to 32 %.
To finish first-line treatment after a hypersensitivity reaction, choose one of the specified alternative regimens.

alternative_regimens.name: cisplatin/vincristine (A) with cyclophosphamide/ vincristine (B)
alternative_regimens.summary: Alternative specified by the LGG2004 protocol for completing first-line treatment after carboplatin hypersensitivity.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Carboplatin hypersensitivity during first-line treatment; administration every 6 weeks.

alternative_regimens.name: vinblastine
alternative_regimens.summary: Switch to weekly monotherapy to complete first-line treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pediatric patients ≥1 year of age with low-grade glioma requiring systemic therapy.
decision_rules: The guide reports FDA and EMA approval of dabrafenib plus trametinib as first-line treatment for this population.
Consider the unresolved optimal duration and potentially unknown very late effects of targeted treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: dabrafenib plus trametinib
recommended_regimens.summary: Approved first-line combination for eligible patients with BRAF V600E mutation. The cited comparative trial studied pLGG with BRAF V600 mutations needing first-line non-surgical therapy.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The cited trial reported significantly more responses and longer PFS with dabrafenib-trametinib than with carboplatin plus vincristine; the document does not give numerical estimates for these outcomes.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Other first-line comparisons of targeted therapy against standard chemotherapy remain under investigation in clinical trials.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with LGG that has relapsed after first-line therapy.
decision_rules: The guide reports FDA approval of tovorafenib for LGG with a RAF alteration after relapse following first-line treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: tovorafenib
recommended_regimens.summary: The document describes its regulatory approval in this relapse setting; it does not specify a dose or treatment duration.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide identifies tovorafenib as a type II RAF inhibitor and notes unresolved questions about the optimal duration and very late effects of targeted treatments.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with SEGA(s) requiring intervention when the tumour cannot be operated on, surgery is contraindicated, complete resection cannot be achieved surgically, or lesions affect both fornices.
decision_rules: Use a multidisciplinary team to choose medical or surgical intervention.
An mTOR inhibitor is indicated for patients requiring intervention when any of the listed surgical limitations or bilateral fornix lesions applies.

recommended_regimens.name: Everolimus
recommended_regimens.summary: Medical treatment for SEGA in patients with TSC. For age ≥1 year and < 3 years, the stated dose is 7 mg/m2 BSA po once daily; for patients> 3 years, it is 4.5 mg.m2 BSA po once daily. The target trough level is 5–15 ng/ml.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The stated age categories do not specify a dose for patients exactly 3 years old.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients for whom radiotherapy is selected after other management, with particular caution in young children and those with NF1.
decision_rules: Radiotherapy remains a standard salvage treatment; weigh tumour control against late effects.
Chemotherapy can delay or avert radiotherapy to limit cognitive, endocrine and vascular harm and radiation-induced malignancies.
Delay radiotherapy especially in young patients.

recommended_regimens.name: Radiotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Salvage local treatment; modern high-precision techniques, including proton therapy, may limit long-term toxicity. The recommended dose is between 50.4 and 54 Gy. A dose under 54 Gy could reduce vasculopathy risk.

not_recommended.name: Radiotherapy for children with NF1
not_recommended.reason: Avoid it as much as possible because this group has increased risks of second malignancy and late vascular effects.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document identifies patients younger than 5 years of age as apparently at highest risk of sequelae after conformal radiotherapy, neurocognitive decline in children younger than 7 years old in the described setting, and age <10 years as a predisposing factor for vasculopathy. Risk also depends on tumour location, radiation field and doses to vulnerable structures.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected patients with tumours for which even minimal growth could cause substantial morbidity, or with a low expected risk of radiotherapy-related neurocognitive harm; older patients with unresectable diffuse astrocytoma histology or a midbrain/thalamus tumour may also be considered.
decision_rules: Consider up-front radiotherapy only following multidisciplinary tumour board agreement in the specified selected circumstances.
Older patients with unresectable diffuse astrocytoma or a midbrain/thalamus location might benefit from early radiotherapy because their long-term survival may be suboptimal.
Balance this option against late toxicity and the ability to preserve surrounding normal tissue.

recommended_regimens.name: Radiotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: A primary-treatment option in selected cases where surrounding normal tissue can be optimally spared. The recommended dose is between 50.4 and 54 Gy; a dose under 54 Gy could lower vasculopathy risk.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The German SIOP LGG 2004 trial reported 5-year PFS of 80 % in its first-line radiotherapy subgroup; the guide stresses balancing this against treatment-related toxicity.

not_recommended.name: Radiotherapy for children with NF1
not_recommended.reason: Avoid it as much as possible because of increased second-malignancy and late vascular risks.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The cited Fisher series found the same overall survival after 5 and 10 years with radiation immediately after incomplete resection and radiation after progression. Its PFS did not differ by management (P:0.32). Prospective comparisons of modern radiotherapy with systemic treatment are needed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with disseminated disease after chemotherapy has failed.
decision_rules: Craniospinal irradiation may be considered as a treatment option when chemotherapy has failed.

alternative_regimens.name: craniospinal irradiation
alternative_regimens.summary: Potential radiation treatment for disseminated disease after chemotherapy failure.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Disseminated disease in a child when chemotherapy has failed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children< 1 year of age at diagnosis with chiasmatic hypothalamic glioma, regardless of histology or neurological and/or visual symptoms.
decision_rules: A chiasmatic-hypothalamic tumour in an infant below 12 months of age is itself listed as an indication to start non-surgical treatment when the LGG is unresectable.
Assess visual, neurological and endocrine function as well as tumour extent when planning management.

recommended_regimens.name: Carboplatin-Vincristine
recommended_regimens.summary: The guide identifies this as the standard first-line systemic regimen for pLGG but does not prescribe a distinct infant CHG-specific regimen.

recommended_regimens.name: Vinblastine
recommended_regimens.summary: First-line monotherapy used for pLGG in several centres; the guide does not specify a distinct infant CHG-specific schedule.

response_assessment.interpretation: Earlier imaging is suggested for infants or patients with visual threat.

supportive_care: Children with CHG may need replacement of thyroid hormone, hydrocortisone, growth hormone or anti-diuretic hormone, or treatment for precocious puberty.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Infants have additional management challenges. The guide reports that gliomas in this age group are more often hypothalamic or optic-pathway tumours, less amenable to resection, and more likely to be metastatic and progressive.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with a typical intrinsic optic-pathway tumour associated with NF1.
decision_rules: A typical intrinsic tumour does not require biopsy at diagnosis unless a clinical trial needs biological stratification or investigation, or the tumour has atypical features.
Many NF1-related optic-pathway tumours do not require therapy; use clinical, visual and imaging findings to determine whether observation or treatment is needed.
Consider biopsy, if possible, for NF1-LGG outside the optic pathway when it progresses or has atypical imaging features.

recommended_regimens.name: Observation
recommended_regimens.summary: A management option for NF1-related optic-pathway tumours without an indication for active treatment.

not_recommended.name: Routine biopsy at diagnosis
not_recommended.reason: A typical intrinsic NF1-associated optic-pathway tumour does not require it, except for the stated trial-related or atypical presentations.

not_recommended.name: Radiotherapy
not_recommended.reason: Avoid it as much as possible in children with NF1 because of increased risks of second malignancy and vascular late effects.

response_assessment.method: Age-appropriate visual acuity and visual-field testing, with fundoscopy and OCT.
response_assessment.interpretation: Identify stable, worsening or improving visual function to guide treatment decisions.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: NF1-related tumours generally have better PFS than sporadic optic-pathway tumours, although both can cause visual loss, endocrine problems or hydrocephalus.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children presenting with raised intracranial pressure from a tectal plate glioma.
decision_rules: Address cerebrospinal-fluid obstruction at diagnosis; diversion is usually required.

recommended_regimens.name: endoscopic third ventriculostomy
recommended_regimens.summary: A procedure that can often provide the cerebrospinal-fluid diversion needed at diagnosis.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For pLGG-associated evolving cysts or cerebrospinal-fluid circulation disturbances more broadly, neuroendoscopy with neuronavigation and appropriate shunt technology should be considered as minimally invasive options at diagnosis or during long-term follow-up.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with spinal pLGG for whom an intervention is indicated.
decision_rules: Consider gross total resection when feasible, while recognising that infiltration and indistinct boundaries often prevent complete removal.
If surgery is indicated, perform it with intraoperative neuromonitoring.
Use baseline brain MRI for spinal LGG.

recommended_regimens.name: Gross total resection
recommended_regimens.summary: When achievable, it appears to be the most important factor for PFS in spinal pLGG.

alternative_regimens.name: chemotherapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Chemotherapy, including repeated courses, may help control tumour and reduce morbidity; the guide says it seems to produce tumour control comparable to radiotherapy in this setting.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when tumour control is needed and complete resection is difficult.

response_assessment.interpretation: Establish intracranial status in a patient with spinal LGG.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Spinal pLGG can present with clear deficits or nonspecific symptoms in young children, and diagnosis may be delayed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with cerebral low-grade epilepsy-associated tumours.
decision_rules: Determine whether to operate from imaging appearance, the feasibility of safe resection and refractoriness of epilepsy.
Arrange treatment through a neurosurgical team dedicated to epilepsy surgery.

recommended_regimens.name: surgical treatment
recommended_regimens.summary: A treatment option selected according to tumour anatomy, safe surgical access and seizure burden. The cited studies identified shorter symptom duration, partial/focal seizures and gross total excision as predictors of a good seizure outcome.

response_assessment.method: Neurological examination and evaluation of epilepsy control.
response_assessment.interpretation: Compare subsequent neurological function with baseline and assess seizure outcome.

supportive_care: Continue epilepsy medication when indicated and check for interactions with anticancer and supportive-care medicines.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with a cervico-medullary pLGG requiring treatment.
decision_rules: Direct treatment toward local tumour control while preserving, or potentially restoring, neurological function.

response_assessment.interpretation: Monitor function in the context of a risk of progression or recurrence, including late events.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide does not name a site-specific treatment regimen for this population.

special_populations.considerations: In infants, tumours more often arise in the hypothalamic or optic pathway area (61–67 %), are less amenable to resection, and are more likely to be metastatic (23 %) or progressive than LGG in older children. Infants less than 1 year of age have significantly poorer 10-year OS than older children (71.4 % versus 91.6 %, respectively). Spine MRI is typically recommended for infants with a primary brain pLGG.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Infants below 12 months of age with chiasmatic-hypothalamic tumours meet a listed indication to start non-surgical treatment if the tumour is unresectable. MRI at week 12 may be considered during treatment.

special_populations.population: Children with infant CHG or diencephalic syndrome
special_populations.considerations: Infant CHG denotes a chiasmatic hypothalamic glioma diagnosed in a child < 1 year of age, regardless of histology or neurological or visual symptoms. Diencephalic syndrome involves emaciation despite normal or accelerated linear growth, with BMI or weight for length ≤2 SD, in a young child with a tumour in the chiasmatic-hypothalamic region; it is an additional adverse factor for OS and EFS.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Diencephalic syndrome is a listed indication to start non-surgical treatment for unresectable LGG.

special_populations.considerations: NF1 accounts for 10–20 % of all p LGGs, predominantly optic pathway gliomas. NF1-related optic pathway tumours generally have better PFS than sporadic tumours, and many require no therapy. About ~15 % of children with NF1 have an optic-pathway glioma, often identified through screening; almost 50 % of these remain asymptomatic or nonprogressive.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: A typical intrinsic optic pathway tumour associated with NF1 does not require biopsy at diagnosis unless its features are atypical or a clinical trial requires biological assessment. Biopsy should be considered, if feasible, for an NF1-LGG outside the optic pathway, particularly if it progresses or has atypical imaging features. Radiotherapy should be avoided as much as possible because this population has increased risks of second malignancy and late vascular effects.

special_populations.population: Patients with Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC) and SEGA
special_populations.considerations: TSC is associated with SEGA, which accounts for 1–2 % of pLGGs. The choice between medical and surgical treatment should be made by a multidisciplinary team.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: An mTOR inhibitor is indicated when intervention is required and the tumour cannot be operated on, surgery is contraindicated, complete removal is not possible, or bilateral fornix lesions are present. The stated Everolimus doses for SEGA with TSC are 7 mg/m2 BSA po once daily at age ≥1 year and < 3 years, or 4.5 mg.m2 BSA po once daily for patients> 3 years, targeting trough levels of 5–15 ng/ml.

special_populations.population: Patients with RASopathies other than NF1
special_populations.considerations: Patients with conditions such as Noonan syndrome have an increased risk of pLGGs, mainly dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumors.

special_populations.population: Patients with constitutional mismatch repair syndrome (CMMRD)
special_populations.considerations: CMMRD can produce LGGs that resemble pleomorphic xanthoastrocytomas as well as malignant gliomas. The reported cumulative likelihood of transformation to high-grade gliomas is 100 % in 6 years.

Leptomeningeal dissemination occurs in 4–12 % of children with LGG at diagnosis or progression and is associated with poorer outcomes; reported OS at 5, 10, and 15 years is 80.7 %, 63 %, and 50.9 %, respectively. Leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI also calls for consideration of diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumour (DLGNT).
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Outside infancy, spine MRI and CSF examination for neoplastic cells are generally reserved for concern about metastatic disease or, in some cases, clinical-trial participation. Craniospinal irradiation may be an option for children with disseminated disease after chemotherapy has failed.

special_populations.population: Young children being considered for radiotherapy
special_populations.considerations: Patients younger than 5 years of age appear to have the greatest risk of sequelae after conformal radiotherapy. Neurocognitive decline has been observed in children with LGG younger than 7 years old when tumour location results in greater volume and/or dose to the left temporal lobe or hippocampus, even with proton therapy and regardless of NF1 status. Age <10 years has also been identified as a factor predisposing to vasculopathies.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Younger age limits selection of radiotherapy as first-line treatment, so radiotherapy is particularly delayed in young patients.

special_populations.population: Patients with optic pathway or chiasmatic-hypothalamic tumours and visual impairment
special_populations.considerations: NF1-related and sporadic tumours can cause visual loss, endocrine disorders, hypothalamic symptoms and, if the third ventricle is obstructed, hydrocephalus. Younger age at presentation, optic nerve atrophy at presentation and postchiasmatic involvement are considered risk factors for visual deficit. Assessment of visual acuity, visual fields, fundoscopy and increasingly OCT informs treatment decisions and evaluation of visual change, although examination can be difficult in young or uncooperative children.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For unresectable LGG, listed ophthalmologic indications for non-surgical treatment include definitive or borderline vision loss, deterioration of remaining low-level vision or visual field, nystagmus due to visual impairment in an infant, any loss in the second eye when the first is blind, and deterioration during follow-up of more than or equal to 0.2 LogMAR. Well-accessible exophytic portions of these generally unresectable tumours may be partly removed to improve tumour control.

special_populations.population: Children with CHG requiring hormone substitution
special_populations.considerations: Children with CHG may require thyroid hormone, hydrocortisone, growth hormone or anti-diuretic hormone replacement, and may receive treatment for precocious puberty. A retrospective study of 124 patients with midline pLGG found no statistically significant increase in relapse risk among recipients of growth hormonal replacement therapy compared with nonrecipients; prospective evidence on its safety is still needed.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Hormonal therapy may continue during chemotherapy without adjustment. Whether to stop growth hormone replacement is decided under institutional guidelines because conclusive evidence is lacking.

special_populations.population: Patients with tumours in surgically high-risk or eloquent brain regions
special_populations.considerations: Location and the risk of lasting neurological injury constrain resection. In the posterior fossa, surgery carries risks including cerebellar mutism syndrome, cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome and cranial nerve dysfunction. Tumours in the supratentorial midline, optic pathway/hypothalamus or brainstem often favour a more limited surgical approach.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: A multidisciplinary tumour board should weigh surgical benefit against risk. Biopsy or resection in surgically high-risk brain regions is recommended only when performed by paediatric neurosurgeons experienced in operating there. Partial resection or biopsy is often more appropriate than complete removal in the listed eloquent locations.

special_populations.population: Patients with cerebral low-grade epilepsy-associated tumours (LEATs)
special_populations.considerations: Surgical decisions take account of imaging appearance, the feasibility of safe removal and epilepsy refractoriness. Shorter symptom duration, partial/focal seizures and gross total excision were predictors of a favourable seizure outcome.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: These patients are also treated by dedicated epilepsy neurosurgical teams.

special_populations.considerations: Symptoms can be subtle in young children, delaying diagnosis. Infiltration and indistinct margins can prevent complete removal. Even late progression or recurrence is a concern for cervico-medullary pLGGs.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: A baseline brain MRI should be performed for spinal LGG. If spinal tumour resection is indicated, it must use intraoperative neuromonitoring. Gross total resection, when feasible, appears most important for PFS; repeated chemotherapy may help control tumour and reduce morbidity and seems to provide tumour control comparable with radiotherapy. Treatment of cervico-medullary pLGGs should pursue local control while preserving or restoring neurological function.

special_populations.considerations: IDH1 mutations are rare in pLGG. COG reported an incidence of 16 % in adolescents over the age of 14 years; their clinical implications in children remain uncertain.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Testing for IDH1 mutations may be considered, particularly in adolescents.

special_populations.population: Patients receiving Vinblastine with a small BSA
special_populations.considerations: In the published series, the recommended vinblastine dose was 6 mg/m2, but almost 70 % of patients required a reduction because of haematological toxicity. The proposed starting doses have not been tested in protocols with published data.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: The proposed weekly iv push starting dose is 0, 17 mg/kg BW for BSA<0,6 m2, or 5 mg/m2 (max:10 mg/dose) for BSA≥0.6 m2.

recommendations.statement: For infants with LGG, obtain a spine MRI; for other patients, obtain one when metastatic disease is suspected or when required for participation in a clinical trial.
Use the same indications for CSF examination for neoplastic cells as for spine MRI: infancy, concern for metastatic disease, or a relevant clinical trial.
When MRI shows leptomeningeal enhancement, include diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumour (DLGNT) in the differential diagnosis.
For a spinal pLGG requiring resection, use intraoperative neuromonitoring.
recommendations.context: Resection can be difficult when the tumour infiltrates adjacent tissue and its margins are indistinct.
recommendations.rationale: The aim is to limit neurological injury during surgery.

recommendations.statement: In a child with a suspected LGG involving the hypothalamus, particularly an older child or one with diabetes insipidus, consider an intracranial germ cell tumor in the differential diagnosis and include germ cell tumour markers and the distinguishing imaging features of GCTs and LGG in the work-up.
recommendations.context: Endocrine symptoms and lesions of the anterior visual pathways.
recommendations.rationale: Intracranial germ cell tumors can also involve the anterior visual pathways.

recommendations.statement: Obtain contrast-enhanced MR imaging when the tumour is diagnosed.

Obtain a presurgical baseline MRI for every patient and, after surgery, an MRI within 24–72 h to assess residual tumour, unless a suitable intraoperative or immediate postoperative MRI has already been performed.
recommendations.context: Imaging at diagnosis and following resection.
recommendations.rationale: The postoperative study establishes the extent of residual disease.

recommendations.statement: If surgery is not indicated or only a small biopsy is obtained, the diagnostic or prebiopsy MRI may be used as the pretreatment baseline.
If extensive postoperative parenchymal changes obscure possible residual tumour and treatment is urgently indicated, consider another MRI approximately 2–3 weeks after surgery.
recommendations.context: Postoperative assessment in line with RAPNO Working Group recommendations.
recommendations.rationale: Later imaging may define residual disease more clearly.

recommendations.statement: For a primary brain pLGG, obtain spine MRI in infants or when metastatic disease is suspected; perform it before surgery or 10–14 days afterward.
Obtain a baseline brain MRI for spinal LGG.
If feasible, use the safest available contrast agent, currently a macrocyclic gadolinium-based contrast agent, and retain the same agent throughout surveillance when possible.
recommendations.rationale: This is intended to reduce nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk and tissue deposition.

recommendations.statement: Contrast agents are used as standard practice during LGG follow-up regardless of time since diagnosis, resection status, histological diagnosis, or tumour enhancement; in the uncommon case of a completely non-enhancing pLGG, surveillance MRI without contrast may be considered.
recommendations.context: The exception reflects a RAPNO working group comment.

recommendations.statement: Include histomorphological assessment of FFPE tumour tissue using HE-, PAS-, Alcianblue- and Reticulin-staining and select an IHC panel according to tumour differentiation.
Include IDH 1(R132H) and BRAFV600E in additional pathology testing to distinguish gliomas that may have different biological behaviour.
Assess H3K27M in midline or spinal tumours to distinguish unexpected high-grade disease.
Use molecular pathology as part of standard care for pLGG; methylation profiling can support classification.
recommendations.rationale: Molecular findings can inform management of different pLGG subtypes.

recommendations.statement: Test for the absence of H3K27M mutations in brain stem and midline thalamic tumours and of H3G34R/H3G34V in cerebral hemisphere tumours.
recommendations.rationale: These alterations occur in high-grade gliomas, which the testing is intended to distinguish.

recommendations.statement: Consider testing for IDH1 mutations, most frequently at position p. R132, particularly in adolescents.
recommendations.rationale: The long-term clinical implications of IDH1 mutations in children remain uncertain.

recommendations.statement: When feasible, consider participation in the LOGGIC Core Bioclinical Data Bank.
recommendations.context: European collection of clinical data and tumour tissue from patients with pLGG.

recommendations.statement: Perform a baseline neurological examination and use it subsequently to assess stable function, deterioration, or improvement, as well as epilepsy control.
recommendations.context: Decision-making about observation or treatment and assessment of neurological response.
recommendations.rationale: Baseline findings help determine whether treatment is indicated.

recommendations.statement: Assess visual acuity and visual fields with age-appropriate methods, supported by fundoscopy and OCT, particularly when the optic pathway is involved.
recommendations.rationale: Visual findings inform treatment decisions and assessment of change over time.

recommendations.statement: Follow the published REiNS and pLGGs International Consensus recommendations when assessing visual outcomes.
Include systematic examination of eye position, movement range, smooth pursuit, saccades, gaze holding, optokinetic nystagmus, and other forms of nystagmus in the clinical visual assessment.
recommendations.context: Evaluation of possible ocular motor dysfunction.
recommendations.rationale: Eye-movement abnormalities can reflect tumour location or cranial nerve dysfunction.

recommendations.statement: Make treatment and follow-up decisions through a multidisciplinary tumour board that meets regularly and includes neuro-oncology, neurosurgery, neurology, neuroradiology, radiation oncology, and neuropathology expertise; involve ophthalmology, audiology, endocrinology, and neuropsychology as appropriate.
recommendations.rationale: Decisions require interpretation across specialties.

recommendations.statement: Consider starting non-surgical treatment for unresectable LGG when tumour volume increases by > 25 % under RAPNO working group criteria, a previously unaffected area becomes involved, a new lesion appears, or metastases increase in number or size; record optic nerve diameter increase separately.

Consider starting non-surgical treatment for unresectable LGG in the presence of diencephalic syndrome, a focal neurological deficit or focal increased intracranial pressure following tumour growth, drug-resistant seizures with or without tumour growth, or symptomatic metastases.
Start non-surgical treatment for an unresectable chiasmatic-hypothalamic tumour in an infant below 12 months of age.

Consider starting non-surgical treatment for unresectable LGG with definite vision loss, borderline vision described as a threat to vision, reduced remaining low-level vision or visual field, visually related nystagmus in an infant, any loss in the second eye when the first is blind, or visual deterioration during follow-up; a significant loss is more than or equal to 0.2 LogMAR.

Use an mTOR inhibitor for SEGA(s) requiring intervention when the tumour cannot be operated on, surgery is contraindicated, complete resection is not possible, or bilateral fornix lesions are present.
Use surgical resection as the principal treatment for LGG when feasible, with planning informed by anatomical location, imaging demarcation, and histology.
If an experienced paediatric neurosurgeon does not recommend resection, thoroughly consider biopsy for a symptomatic tumour, except in NF1-related OPG.
recommendations.rationale: Biopsy can establish histological and molecular features relevant to management.

recommendations.statement: Use multidisciplinary tumour board discussion to decide whether to biopsy or resect, and how extensively, both at diagnosis and at progression.
recommendations.context: Balance the anticipated therapeutic benefit against surgical risk and the need to identify histological and molecular subtype.
recommendations.rationale: Long-term survival and preservation of quality of life are important considerations.

recommendations.statement: Use gross total resection as the initial therapeutic approach when applicable; for posterior fossa tumours, discuss surgical risks in the multidisciplinary setting.
recommendations.rationale: Posterior fossa surgery carries risks including cerebellar mutism syndrome, cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome, and cranial nerve dysfunction.

recommendations.statement: For tumours in the supratentorial midline, optic pathway/hypothalamus, or brainstem, consider partial resection or biopsy rather than complete resection when the eloquence of the location makes that more appropriate.
recommendations.rationale: These tumour locations involve functionally important structures.

recommendations.statement: Have biopsy or resection in surgically high-risk brain regions performed only by paediatric neurosurgeons experienced in operating in those regions.

Do not routinely biopsy a typical intrinsic optic pathway tumour associated with NF1 at diagnosis, unless atypical features are present or a clinical trial requires biological stratification or addresses a relevant biological question.
Consider biopsy, if feasible, for NF1-LGG outside the optic pathway, especially when it is progressing or has atypical imaging features.

For cerebral LEATs, base the surgical decision on imaging appearance, the feasibility of safe tumour removal, and whether epilepsy is refractory; involve a neurosurgical team dedicated to epilepsy surgery.
When a pLGG is near an eloquent area, consider intraoperative MRI or monitoring and, when relevant, a surgical second opinion or discussion.
recommendations.context: Planning surgery near functionally important structures.

recommendations.statement: Consider neuroendoscopy with neuronavigation and appropriate shunt technology as minimally invasive options for evolving tumour cysts or CSF-circulation disturbances, both at diagnosis and during long-term follow-up.
recommendations.context: Management of associated cysts or CSF-circulation problems.

recommendations.statement: For first-line treatment using Carboplatin-Vincristine, administer the European induction and consolidation schedule over 81 weeks.
recommendations.context: Chemotherapy regimen described in Annex A.

recommendations.statement: Remain alert for carboplatin hypersensitivity during repeated exposure. To complete first-line therapy after such a reaction, alternatives are cisplatin/vincristine (A) with cyclophosphamide/ vincristine (B) every 6 weeks under the LGG2004 protocol, or a switch to weekly vinblastine monotherapy.
recommendations.context: Carboplatin hypersensitivity reaction, reported at rates between 6 % and 32 %.
recommendations.rationale: The likelihood of hypersensitivity rises with repeated carboplatin exposure.

recommendations.statement: When Vinblastine is selected as first-line therapy, continue it for a total treatment duration of 70 weeks.
The proposed starting dose for weekly vinblastine is 0, 17 mg/kg BW by iv push for BSA<0,6 m2, or 5 mg/m2 (max:10 mg/dose) by iv push for BSA≥0.6 m2.
recommendations.context: This proposed starting dose has not been tested in protocols with published data; the published-series dose was 6 mg/m2, with a reduction needed in almost 70 % of patients because of haematological toxicity.

recommendations.statement: For a paediatric patient ≥1 year of age with low-grade glioma bearing a BRAF V600E mutation and requiring systemic therapy, dabrafenib plus trametinib is an approved first-line option.
recommendations.context: The document reports FDA and EMA approval; optimal treatment duration and very late effects remain uncertain.

recommendations.statement: Have the multidisciplinary team decide between medical treatment and surgery for SEGA.

For SEGA with TSC, administer Everolimus at 7 mg/m2 BSA po once daily for patients aged ≥1 year and < 3 years, or 4.5 mg.m2 BSA po once daily for patients> 3 years, targeting trough levels of 5–15 ng/ml.
Delay radiotherapy particularly in younger patients when selecting treatment for pLGG.
recommendations.rationale: Younger age is associated with greater concern about neurocognitive and vascular late effects.

recommendations.statement: Use radiotherapy as a salvage treatment or as primary treatment in selected cases where surrounding normal tissue can be optimally spared; the recommended dose is between 50.4 and 54 Gy.
recommendations.rationale: Lowering the dose to under 54 Gy could reduce vasculopathy risk.

recommendations.statement: Following multidisciplinary tumour board agreement, consider upfront radiotherapy when minimal tumour growth would pose a high risk of substantial morbidity or when the risk of radiotherapy-related neurocognitive effects is low.
For children with disseminated disease, consider craniospinal irradiation as a treatment option if chemotherapy has failed.
Avoid radiotherapy as far as possible in children with NF1.
recommendations.rationale: This group has increased risks of second malignancy and late vascular effects.

recommendations.statement: Before each treatment course, perform a physical examination, anthropometric measurements, a blood count including neutrophils, and the listed biochemical tests; perform a neurological examination every three months and at the end of therapy.
recommendations.context: Proposed assessment schedule in Table 2; the biochemical tests listed are Electrolytes, create, SGOT, SGPT, Ca,Mg,P, Bil.

recommendations.statement: During treatment, perform brain MRI, with spinal MRI when applicable, at week 24,54 and 84 or every 3–6 months until the end of therapy according to institutional policy; consider MRI at week 12 for infants or patients whose vision is threatened.
During treatment, assess ophthalmologic function Every 3 months if the optic pathway is involved, or earlier when clinically indicated.
For a platinum-based regimen, include GFR* and audiometry when anatomically indicated in the proposed assessment schedule.
recommendations.context: Table 2 indicates baseline and end-of-therapy assessment and a six-monthly interval during treatment. The document's two presentations assign conflicting footnote letters to the six-monthly GFR* and audiometry entries; their association with the interval is therefore uncertain.

recommendations.statement: Continue indicated hormone replacement during chemotherapy without routine adjustment; decide whether to stop growth hormone replacement according to institutional guidance.
recommendations.rationale: Conclusive evidence on the safety of growth hormone replacement in LGG is lacking.

recommendations.statement: Generally continue indicated epilepsy medication and check for interactions involving anti-epileptic and supportive-care drugs.
recommendations.rationale: Some anti-epileptic drugs may interact with treatment.

recommendations.statement: Individualise LGG follow-up according to age, NF1 status, primary tumour site, extent of resection, integrated pathological diagnosis, treatment, and relapse history and timing; consider less frequent imaging after the 5th year for patients with gross total resection.
recommendations.rationale: Late relapse can occur, although it is rare.

recommendations.statement: For the observation group without residual tumour or with stable disease, including stable postoperative residue, follow the proposed schedule: physical and neurological examination with auxology every 3 months in the 1st year, every 3–6 months in the 2nd year, every 6 months in the 3rd-5th year, and annually in the 6th-10th year; obtain cranial and/or spinal MRI every 3–6 months in the 1st and 2nd years, every 6–12 months in the 3rd-5th year, and annually in the 6th-10th year.

In the proposed follow-up schedule, perform ophthalmologic assessment for OPG every 3 months in the 1st year, every 3–6 months in the 2nd year, every 6 (-12) months in the 3rd-5th year, and every 6–12 months in the 6th-10th year.
recommendations.context: Table 3 identifies ophthalmology follow-up as mandatory for OPG.

recommendations.statement: For patients with chiasmatic-hypothalamic gliomas under observation, assess endocrine function annually until growth is complete, more often if clinically indicated, and every 3–5 years after growth is complete.

After platinum-based chemotherapy, assess renal function 6 months after treatment ends and yearly thereafter unless another interval is indicated; assessments may be stopped if results are repeatedly normal.

For chemotherapy patients with chiasmatic-hypothalamic tumours, assess endocrine function at the beginning and at 6,12 and 18 months of treatment; for other patients, assess it at the beginning and end. Until growth is complete, continue annual assessment or more often if clinically indicated; after growth is complete, assess every 3–5 years.
recommendations.context: Suggested chemotherapy-group endocrine surveillance in Table 3.

recommendations.statement: After radiotherapy, assess endocrine function at treatment completion and one year later, then annually until growth is complete or more frequently if indicated; after growth is complete, assess every 3 (to 5) years, more frequently if the pituitary-hypothalamic region was in the radiation field.
Plan neurocognitive follow-up according to institutional policy, taking account of tumour location and treatment; it may be omitted for a spinal tumour that does not need treatment.
recommendations.context: Qualification accompanying the proposed follow-up schedule in Table 3.

conditions.name: Paediatric low-grade gliomas (pLGG)
conditions.description: A heterogeneous group of WHO grade 1 and 2 tumours that may have a prolonged course despite generally favourable survival. When complete resection is not possible, progression, repeated treatment and tumour-related brain injury can contribute to chronic impairment even without radiological progression.
conditions.epidemiology: These are the most common brain tumours in childhood, accounting for approximately 35 % during the first year of life and up to 50 % in older children. Reported 10-year overall survival (OS) is between 85 % and 96 %. Anatomical distribution includes midline supratentorial structures in 39–40 %, the cerebellum in 32–36 %, cerebral cortex in 13.1–18.0 %, brainstem in 8.3–10 % and spinal cord in 3.5–4.5 %.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Presentation varies with tumour location and can change over time. Possible findings include raised intracranial pressure, obstructive hydrocephalus, headache, nausea or vomiting, focal neurological or cognitive deficits, seizures, visual impairment and endocrine disturbance. Increased head circumference may be the only presenting sign in an infant. Some tumours are detected during surveillance for a cancer predisposition syndrome. Long-term neurological, visual, endocrine, cognitive and functional difficulties can arise from the tumour, its treatment or both.

conditions.name: optic pathway gliomas

conditions.clinical_presentation: Visual findings range from no symptoms to severe loss. Reduced visual acuity is the most common finding; possible field abnormalities include central scotoma, bitemporal hemianopsia and peripheral contraction. Optic nerve involvement can produce monocular visual loss, while chiasmatic involvement can cause bilateral deterioration, field loss and nystagmus. Visual risk factors identified in the document are younger age at presentation, optic nerve atrophy at presentation and postchiasmatic involvement.
