document_sections.heading: A B S T R A C T
document_sections.content: Pediatric low-grade gliomas are the most frequent brain tumors of childhood and adolescence. Survival is generally favorable, but repeated treatment and lasting complications can make the disease chronic. These recommendations address primary diagnosis within the European Reference Network PaedCan framework. They cover variation by tumor site, age, cancer predisposition, infantile chiasmatic hypothalamic glioma and diencephalic syndrome; diagnostic and treatment criteria; histopathology and molecular pathology; multidisciplinary care; European first-line treatments, adverse effects and follow-up.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Paediatric low-grade gliomas (pLGG) comprise diverse WHO grade 1 and 2 tumors. They account for approximately 35 % of childhood brain tumors during the first year of life and up to 50 % in older children. Reported 10-year overall survival (OS) is between 85 % and 96 %. Neurological, visual, endocrine, cognitive and functional problems may persist because of the tumor, its treatment or both. When complete removal is impossible, progression, further treatment or worsening tumor-related brain injury without radiological progression can contribute to acquired brain injury and a chronic disease course. Resection is the principal treatment when feasible. In CCG9891/POG9130, children with confirmed gross total resection had 5-year PFS of 94 % and OS of 99 %; anatomical constraints or metastases prevent complete removal in some patients. Carboplatin and vincristine remain standard first-line systemic therapy: SIOP LGG 2004 reported 5-year OS of 89 % and progression-free survival (PFS) of 46.1 %. A Children’s Oncology Group (COG) schedule with different doses produced similar findings, including 39 % event-free survival (EFS) for non-NF1 patients. The Canadian Group considers first-line vinblastine monotherapy standard care when chemotherapy is needed; its reported 5-year PFS was 42 % in non-NF1 patients, and many European centers also use it first-line. Radiotherapy was formerly preferred for symptomatic unresectable disease. The German SIOP LGG 2004 first-line radiotherapy subgroup had 5-year PFS of 80 %, weighed against potential neurocognitive, neurological, endocrine and vascular harm and second malignancy. Late-effect risk depends on age, tumor site, radiation field and doses reaching the left temporal lobe, left hippocampus or hypothalamic-pituitary region. Fisher’s series reported equal OS at 5 and 10 years for radiotherapy immediately after incomplete resection versus radiotherapy after progression; PFS did not differ by management (P:0.32). PFS at 3 and 5 years was 58 %±5 % and 48 %±5 % with observation, 56 %±6 % and 48 % ±6 % with immediate radiotherapy, and 43 %±13 % and 36 %±13 % with immediate chemotherapy. A Canadian population-based retrospective study of 1202 patients, with median follow-up of 12.73 years, raised concern about an association between upfront radiotherapy and increased delayed overall and tumor-related deaths. Recognition of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPk) pathway involvement prompted targeted-treatment research. MEK inhibitors, including selumetinib and trametinib, and RAF-inhibitors have been studied in phase 1 and 2 trials, with randomized phase 3 trials continuing. In first-line nonsurgical treatment of tumors with BRAFV600 mutations, dabrafenib-trametinib produced significantly more responses and longer PFS than carboplatin plus vincristine. At least four trials are comparing first-line standard chemotherapy with targeted therapy in BRAF-altered or other pLGG: LOGGIC-Firefly 2, PLGG-METRIC, ACNS1831 for NF1-related LGGs and ACNS1833; some exclude V600E BRAF mutation. Tumor-control choices should also protect neurological, visual, endocrine and functional outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 2. Background of European Standard Clinical Practice Project and methodology
document_sections.content: European Reference Networks (ERNs) connect European healthcare providers to improve care for complex or rare conditions requiring specialist expertise. PaedCan was among the 24 ERNs approved in December 2016 and aims to reduce geographic inequalities in childhood cancer survival through accessible, high-quality, cost-effective cross-border care. The European Standard Clinical Practice (ESCP) Project joins ERN PaedCan with European Society for Paediatric Oncology (SIOP Europe’s or SIOPe) Clinical Trial Groups to describe current practice for common childhood cancers. SIOPe Brain Tumor Group (BTG) initiated the brain-tumor protocols with the relevant disease working groups. The review authors initially drafted the primary pLGG recommendations; the LGG WG approved them, ERN PaedCan and SIOPe board members reviewed them, and the recommendations were approved for publication in the members’ portal.

document_sections.heading: 3. Patient groups
document_sections.content: Patients with LGG are characterized by tumor location, age, underlying cancer predisposition and metastatic status. Management also separates patients suitable for observation from those needing treatment.

document_sections.heading: ● Location of the tumour
document_sections.content: Reported anatomical distributions are 39–40 % in supratentorial midline structures, including the hypothalamus, optic chiasm and nerves, ventricles and other midline sites; 32–36 % in the cerebellum; 13.1–18.0 % in the cerebral cortex; 8.3–10 % in the brainstem; and 3.5–4.5 % in the spinal cord. Resectability depends on site, tumor grade and the risk of lasting neurological injury. Hemispheric and cerebellar tumors are often operable, but perirolandic, mesial temporal or dominant-language locations can make surgery harmful. After cerebellar LGG surgery, patients can have fine-motor, coordination, sensory, oculomotor, cognitive or learning deficits. Posterior-fossa resection can also cause cerebellar mutism syndrome, though less often than medulloblastoma surgery, particularly with involvement of the middle cerebellar peduncle, dentate nucleus or fourth-ventricle floor. Chiasmatic hypothalamic gliomas (CHG) and other optic pathway gliomas may be NF1-related or sporadic, with differing natural history and imaging. NF1-related tumors generally have better PFS, and many need no treatment. Either type can cause visual loss, endocrine disease, hypothalamic symptoms including diencephalic syndrome in young children, or hydrocephalus from third-ventricle obstruction. Complete resection is generally not feasible, although accessible exophytic portions may be removed to improve control. Thalamic pLGGs account for 1–2 % and often present with hemiplegia and/or hemianopsia. Tectal plate gliomas occur predominantly in children, constitute 5 % of pediatric brainstem tumors and typically present with raised intracranial pressure; CSF diversion is usually needed at diagnosis and can often be accomplished by endoscopic third ventriculostomy. Cervico-medullary pLGGs grow slowly and present with lower-brainstem symptoms. Long-term survival is high, but progression or recurrence, including late recurrence, is common; treatment should control local disease while preserving or restoring neurological function. Spinal pLGGs are uncommon and insidious. Young children may have either definite deficits or vague symptoms, delaying diagnosis until symptoms become severe. Infiltration and poorly defined tissue boundaries can obstruct complete removal; indicated resection requires intraoperative neuromonitoring. Feasible gross total resection appears most important for PFS. Repeated chemotherapy may help control disease and lessen morbidity and appears to provide tumor control comparable with radiotherapy.

document_sections.heading: ● Age
document_sections.content: Infant pLGG has a distinct clinical profile and additional management difficulties. Tumors are more often hypothalamic or optic-pathway lesions (61–67 %), restricting resection, and are more often metastatic (23 %) or progressive than tumors in older children. Children diagnosed before 1 year have significantly worse OS than older children: 10-year OS is 71.4 % versus 91.6 %, respectively. Infant CHG denotes any LGG histology at a chiasmatic-hypothalamic location diagnosed at < 1 year, regardless of neurological or visual symptoms. Diencephalic syndrome in young children with a chiasmatic-hypothalamic tumor consists of emaciation despite normal-to-accelerated linear growth and BMI or weight for length ≤2 SD; it is an additional unfavorable factor for both OS and EFS.

document_sections.heading: • Underlying cancer predisposition syndromes
document_sections.content: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) accounts for 10–20 % of all pLGGs, predominantly optic-pathway tumors. Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC) is associated with Subependymal Giant Cell Astrocytoma (SEGA), which accounts for 1–2 % of pLGGs. Other RASopathies include Noonan syndrome, with increased pLGG risk, chiefly dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumors. Constitutional mismatch repair syndrome (CMMRD) can produce malignant gliomas or LGGs resembling pleomorphic xanthoastrocytomas; the reported cumulative likelihood of high-grade transformation is 100 % in 6 years.

document_sections.heading: • Presence of metastasis
document_sections.content: Leptomeningeal dissemination occurs at diagnosis or progression in 4–12 % of children with LGG and is associated with poorer outcomes: OS at 5, 10, and 15 years is 80.7 %, 63 %, and 50.9 %, respectively. Spine MRI is typically recommended for infants and otherwise when metastatic disease is suspected or, in some circumstances, for trial participation; the same approach applies to CSF testing for neoplastic cells. Diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumour (DLGNT) should always be considered when MRI shows leptomeningeal enhancement.

document_sections.heading: 4. Diagnostic criteria
document_sections.content: Diagnosis draws on the clinical presentation, imaging, tissue and molecular findings, and baseline neurological, visual and endocrine assessment.

document_sections.heading: 4.1. Clinical presentation
document_sections.content: Symptoms depend strongly on tumor location, can evolve and may be atypical or attributed to another condition, potentially delaying diagnosis. A patient may have one or several of the presentations described below.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.1. Symptom-free via screening or other reason for MRI
document_sections.content: Incidental brain tumors in children without corresponding symptoms are increasingly found as imaging is used for indications such as trauma or headache. They occur in 0.2 – 5.7 % of brain images and can substantially burden patients, families and caregivers. Most are presumed LGG, but usually lack histological confirmation and fall outside these recommendations. Surveillance imaging for cancer predisposition can also reveal pLGG. Approximately ~15 % of children with NF1 are estimated to have an optic-pathway glioma, often identified by screening; almost 50 % remain asymptomatic or nonprogressive.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.2. Neurology [63]
document_sections.content: Ventricular-outflow obstruction, especially from cerebellar or tectal lesions, can cause raised intracranial pressure and obstructive hydrocephalus. Headache and nausea or vomiting are common; increased head circumference may be the sole presenting sign in infants. Focal manifestations include weakness, sensory loss, language or cognitive difficulty, personality change and declining school or athletic performance. Cortical lesions often cause focal deficits or seizures. Brainstem lesions can produce fatigue, ataxia and multiple cranial neuropathies. Cerebellar lesions can cause impaired coordination or balance, raised-pressure signs and/or 6th cranial nerve palsy. Some posterior-fossa tumors extend through cerebellar peduncles into both brainstem and cerebellum; involvement of the area postrema can cause vomiting without other signs of raised pressure. Frontal, temporal and parietal tumors are more often associated with seizures than occipital tumors, and cortical lesions more often than deeper noncortical lesions. Gangliogliomas and dysplastic neuroepithelial tumours can be associated with chronic drug-resistant epilepsy. Infratentorial tumors seldom cause seizures.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.3. Vision
document_sections.content: Optic-pathway gliomas can cause anything from no visual symptoms to severe loss. Reduced acuity is the most common manifestation; possible field abnormalities include central scotoma, bitemporal hemianopsia and peripheral constriction. Optic-nerve glioma can cause monocular loss. Optic-tract tumors, described more often with NF1, can cause unilateral loss, strabismus and/or proptosis, whereas optic-radiation tumors can cause homonymous hemianopia. Chiasmatic disease can cause bilateral deterioration, field loss, nystagmus and ultimately reduced acuity. Acuity and field testing, fundoscopy and increasingly optical coherence tomography (OCT) are important but challenging in young or uncooperative children. Younger age at presentation, pre-existing optic-nerve atrophy and postchiasmatic involvement are considered risk factors for visual deficit.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.4. Endocrine disorders
document_sections.content: Hypothalamic LGG can initially manifest through altered weight or growth, early or delayed puberty, and, very rarely, polydipsia or polyuria with diabetes insipidus. Intracranial germ cell tumors rarely affect the anterior visual pathways but belong in the differential diagnosis, particularly for older children or those with diabetes insipidus; assessment should include germ cell tumor markers and distinguishing imaging features of GCTs and LGG. Diencephalic syndrome in young patients with suprasellar midline LGG involves disordered metabolism, failure to thrive, severe emaciation and near-absence of subcutaneous fat.

document_sections.heading: 4.2. Imaging
document_sections.content: Magnetic resonance imaging is the preferred modality for assessing central nervous system neoplasms, and contrast-enhanced MR should be obtained at diagnosis. Grade 1 pLGG is usually well circumscribed, T1-hypointense and T2-hyperintense. Grade 1 astrocytomas frequently enhance uniformly with gadolinium, whereas grade 2 diffuse astrocytomas usually do not enhance and may be less sharply bounded.

document_sections.heading: At diagnosis
document_sections.content: All patients should have presurgical baseline MRI and postoperative MRI within 24–72 h to determine residual tumor, unless an adequate intraoperative or immediate postoperative scan is available. If surgery is not indicated or only a small biopsy is obtained, diagnostic or prebiopsy MRI may provide the pretreatment baseline. When extensive postoperative parenchymal change obscures residual disease and treatment is urgently indicated, another MRI approximately 2–3 weeks after surgery may better define the residue, as recommended by the RAPNO Working Group. For primary brain pLGG, spine MRI is recommended in infants and when metastasis is suspected, including symptoms suggestive of spinal disease, before surgery or 10–14 days afterward. Spinal LGG requires baseline brain MRI. If possible, use the safest available contrast agents, currently macrocyclic gadolinium-based agents, to reduce nephrogenic systemic fibrosis and tissue deposition, including in the brain; using the same agent throughout surveillance is also preferred when possible. Standard follow-up currently includes contrast regardless of time since diagnosis, completeness of removal, histology or tumor enhancement. RAPNO notes that noncontrast surveillance may be considered in the rare completely nonenhancing pLGG. The document points to additional SIOPe imaging recommendations.

document_sections.heading: 4.3. Histopathology
document_sections.content: LGG comprises heterogeneous glial tumors, including astrocytic and/or oligodendroglial forms, and tumors with mixed neuronal-glial morphology. Under the previous WHO classification they were grades I and II; distinguishing features from high-grade glioma included morphology or, for diffuse glioma, lack of necrosis, mitoses and microvascular proliferation. The 2021 WHO Classification for CNS tumours groups pLGG among Gliomas, Glioneuronal Tumours, and Neuronal Tumours by histological and histogenetic resemblance despite molecular diversity. Histomorphological assessment uses HE-, PAS-, Alcianblue- and Reticulin-staining of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue. Standard immunohistochemistry (IHC), adapted to differentiation, includes glial markers GFAP, Olig2, S100 protein and vimentin; neuronal epitopes synaptophysin, NeuN, chromogranin and neurofilaments when glioneuronal differentiation is present; proliferation markers Ki-67 and phosphor-histone3; CD 68, CD 34 and p53; and, in selected cases, phospho-ERK, phosphor-mTOR and phosphor-AKT. Additional IDH 1(R132H) and BRAFV600E assessment helps distinguish tumors with potentially different behavior; H3K27M assessment in midline or spinal tumors helps identify unexpected high-grade disease. Pilocytic astrocytomas feature marked vascular proliferation, biphasic architecture, Rosenthal fibers, eosinophilic granular bodies and sometimes limited calcification. Gangliogliomas are mixed neuronal-glial grade 1 tumors with granular bodies, calcification, binucleated neurons and cystic degeneration. Most have MAP kinase pathway activation through BRAF p. V600E mutation or alterations including alternative BRAF fusion, RAF1 fusion, KRAS mutation, NF1 mutation or FGFR mutations or fusion. Angiocentric gliomas, seen chiefly in children and young adults, commonly present with refractory epilepsy. They contain monomorphous bipolar cells in an angiocentric pattern, express EMA, GFAP, S100 protein and vimentin, and lack neuronal-antigen immunoreactivity. MYB-QKI fusion occurs in 80–90 %. Diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumors (DLGNT) are rare, show male predominance and usually progress slowly. MRI typically shows leptomeningeal enhancement, not necessarily gross dissemination. Reported changes include chromosomal-arm 1p loss and MAPK/ERK pathway alterations, most often KIAA1549:BRAF fusion (55 %). The account names two molecular subgroups with 1p deletion, DLGNT-MC-1 and DLGNT-MG-2; it describes MC-1 as associated with younger diagnostic age, 19q co-deletion and less aggressive outcome, and says all patients in DLGNT-MC-2 had chromosomal-arm 1q gain. The subgroup labels differ within that account. The document refers readers to additional neuropathology guidance and the 2021 WHO classification for rarer subtypes.

document_sections.heading: 4.4. Molecular pathology [22,76,80,81]
document_sections.content: Methylation profiling can support pLGG classification. Molecular pathology is considered standard care because molecular information can improve management of distinct subtypes. Most pLGGs are driven by a single event that increases RAS/MAPK signaling. Among patients with Neurofibromatosis type 1, 10–15 % develop optic-pathway LGG and another 3–5 % develop LGG elsewhere; a recent study identified additional somatic MAPK-pathway changes alongside germline NF1 changes in many NF1-associated cases. KIAA1549-BRAF fusion is the most frequent pLGG alteration and is significantly enriched in pilocytic astrocytoma and posterior-fossa/cerebellar tumors. BRAFp.V600E mutation frequency varies by histology and site and often co-occurs with CDKN2A deletion. BRAFp.V600E-mutant tumors have worse PFS than KIAA1549-BRAF tumors; coexisting BRAFpV600E mutation and CDKN2A deletion increases the likelihood of malignant behavior. FGFR1 point mutations and kinase-domain duplications occur more often in dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumors, other glioneuronal tumors and midline brain tumors; FGFR1 is the second most commonly altered gene after BRAF. Other BRAF or RAF fusions and rarer alterations involving NTRK, RAF1, ALK and PTNP11 also occur; their prognostic and treatment-response implications remain under investigation. MYB/MYBL1 alterations, often present in angiocentric glioma, appear to identify a pediatric-type diffuse-glioma class. Germline TSC1 and TSC2 mutations are closely linked to subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, present in up to 20 % of patients with tuberous sclerosis complex. Testing for absence of H3K27M mutations in brainstem and midline thalamic tumors and H3G34R/H3G34V in cerebral-hemisphere tumors is recommended to distinguish unexpected high-grade gliomas. IDH1 testing, especially around p. R132, may be considered particularly in adolescents. IDH1 mutations occur in almost 70–90 % of adult WHO grade II and III gliomas and 85 % of secondary GBMs but only 0–17 % of pLGG. COG reported 16 % among adolescents over 14 years, while Ryall et al. found IDH1p.R132H in 0.8 % of 1000 pLGG patients, whose median age at diagnosis was 15.7 years. Their significance in children remains uncertain; these tumors might behave differently over time or represent adult-type malignancies detected early. Integrated profiling has helped distinguish polymorphous low-grade neuroepithelial tumour of the young (PLNTY) and isomorphic diffuse glioma. Sexton-Oates et al. supported methylation profiling as a possible predictor of clinical behavior, and Sturm et al. reported improved recognition of histologically high-grade gliomas with lower-grade molecular profiles. A single molecular-testing strategy is difficult to prescribe: approaches described by Miklja et al. are tiered sequential testing for specific alterations or upfront NGS panels optimized for pLGG. Participation in the LOGGIC Core Bioclinical Data Bank is advised if possible. Additional neuropathology guidance is identified.

document_sections.heading: 4.5. Neurological, visual and endocrine function
document_sections.content: Baseline neurological and ophthalmological findings inform observation or treatment decisions and provide comparators for later functional response. Endocrine assessment is relevant because tumors and their treatment can affect hormonal function.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1. Neurologist
document_sections.content: Baseline neurological examination is crucial for deciding between observation and treatment and assessing epilepsy control. Later examinations use that baseline to classify neurological function as stable, worse or improved.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2. Ophthalmologist
document_sections.content: Visual acuity and field should be tested with age-appropriate methods, supported by fundoscopy and OCT, particularly for optic-pathway tumors. Symptoms and findings in OPG depend on extension, volume, age, raised intracranial pressure and NF1 status. Visual-outcome assessment should follow published REiNS and pLGGs International Consensus recommendations. Baseline ophthalmological findings guide treatment decisions and subsequent assessment of stable, worsening or improved sight. Examination should systematically address eye position and movement range, smooth pursuit, saccades, gaze holding, optokinetic nystagmus and other nystagmus patterns. Isolated vertical eye-movement impairment points to a midbrain lesion; infratentorial tumors can cause ocular-movement disorders through cranial-nerve dysfunction.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.3. Endocrinologist
document_sections.content: Endocrine problems in pLGG can result from tumor, neurosurgery and/or radiotherapy. Suprasellar midline tumors may cause hypothalamic-pituitary (HP) dysfunction. The document identifies separate endocrine-surveillance guidance for children with CNS tumors.

document_sections.heading: 5. Treatment details
document_sections.content: Management decisions depend on multidisciplinary assessment, indications to intervene and the relative benefits and harms of surgery, systemic treatment and radiotherapy.

document_sections.heading: 5.1. Multidisciplinary tumor board
document_sections.content: Decisions about treatment and follow-up require multidisciplinary information and interpretation. A regularly convened board should include neuro-oncology, neurosurgery, neurology, neuroradiology, radiation oncology and neuropathology to optimize diagnosis, surveillance and treatment. Ophthalmology, audiology, endocrinology and neuropsychology input is also highly important.

document_sections.heading: 5.2. Treatment indications
document_sections.content: Table 1 sets out when to begin nonsurgical treatment for unresectable LGG. Its categories are radiological progression, neurological symptoms, infant chiasmatic-hypothalamic disease, ophthalmological deterioration and circumstances warranting an mTOR inhibitor for SEGA(s).

document_sections.heading: 5.3. Treatment modalities
document_sections.content: The treatment options discussed are surgery, first-line chemotherapy, targeted therapy and radiotherapy.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.1. Surgery
document_sections.content: Resection remains the principal LGG treatment when feasible; site, imaging-defined boundaries and histology guide surgery. Microsurgery, neuronavigation, intraoperative imaging with iUS or iMRI, and intraoperative neuromonitoring are important pediatric neuro-oncological tools. If an experienced pediatric neurosurgeon advises against resection, biopsy should be carefully considered for symptomatic tumors, except NF1-related OPG. Molecular findings might eventually inform observation even when no immediate intervention is planned. Neuroendoscopic, stereotactic and robot-assisted biopsy can supply the necessary molecular information. At diagnosis and progression, a multidisciplinary board should balance surgical risks against therapeutic benefit and the value of defining histological and molecular subtype, given expected long survival and the need to preserve quality of life. Gross total resection is the initial approach where suitable. For posterior-fossa tumors, the risks of cerebellar mutism syndrome, cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome and cranial-nerve dysfunction should be considered by the board. Partial removal or biopsy is often more appropriate in eloquent supratentorial midline, optic-pathway/hypothalamic and brainstem sites. Biopsy or resection in high-risk brain regions is recommended only with pediatric neurosurgeons experienced in operating there. Typical intrinsic optic-pathway tumors associated with NF1 do not currently need diagnostic biopsy unless a trial requires biological stratification or an associated biological question, or the tumor has atypical features. Biopsy should be considered when possible for NF1-LGG outside the optic pathway, particularly if progressing or atypical on imaging. For cerebral low-grade epilepsy-associated tumours (LEATs), decisions about surgery consider imaging, safe access and epilepsy refractoriness. Shorter symptomatic duration, partial/focal seizures and gross total excision predicted favorable seizure outcomes in cited studies; dedicated epilepsy-neurosurgery teams treat this group. For eloquent-site pLGG, intraoperative MRI or monitoring may be appropriate, and a second surgical opinion or discussion may be useful. Evolving cysts and disturbed CSF circulation can accompany pLGG; neuroendoscopy with neuronavigation and suitable shunt technology should be considered as minimally invasive options both initially and during long-term follow-up.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2. Chemotherapy first-line treatment regimens
document_sections.content: The first-line chemotherapy regimens described are Carboplatin-Vincristine and Vinblastine.

document_sections.heading: Carboplatin-Vincristine regimen [103]
document_sections.content: Carboplatin-Vincristine is the most frequently used regimen. The European schedule lasts 81 weeks and has induction followed by consolidation. Carboplatin hypersensitivity reaction (HSR) becomes more likely with repeated exposure; reported rates range between 6 % and 32 %. Options for completing first-line therapy after HSR are alternating cisplatin/vincristine (A) with cyclophosphamide/ vincristine (B) every 6 weeks under LGG2004, or changing to weekly vinblastine monotherapy. Further regimen details are provided in the referenced ESCP LGG document.

document_sections.heading: Vinblastine regimen (Annex A)[8]
document_sections.content: First-line Vinblastine is administered to a total treatment duration of 70 weeks. Several centers internationally use monotherapy first-line, initially for NF1 and older patients. Published series recommended 6 mg/m2, but almost 70 % required a lower dose because of hematological toxicity. An untested proposed starting regimen is 0, 17 mg/kg BW for BSA<0,6 m2 or 5 mg/m2 for BSA≥0.6 m2, with max:10 mg/dose, given iv push weekly. The cited ESCP LGG document and Lassaletta et al. provide further details.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.3. Targeted therapy
document_sections.content: Until recently, first-line targeted treatment was acceptable only within clinical trials. Following published findings for dabrafenib plus trametinib in BRAF V600-mutant pLGG, FDA and EMA approved the combination as first-line treatment for pediatric patients ≥1 year who have low-grade glioma with BRAF V600E mutation and need systemic therapy. The EMA information cited was updated on 05/12/2023. Tovorafenib, described as a type II RAF inhibitor, received rare pediatric disease designation for pLGG with an activating RAF alteration and is included in LOGGIC Firefly 2. It also received FDA approval for LGG with RAF alteration after relapse following first-line therapy. Optimal targeted-treatment duration and potentially very late effects remain unknown, requiring further study.

document_sections.heading: Everolimus for patients with SEGA
document_sections.content: A multidisciplinary team should choose between medical and surgical therapy for SEGA. The stated Everolimus dose for SEGA with TSC is 7 mg/m2 BSA po once daily at age ≥1 year and < 3 years, or 4.5 mg.m2 BSA po once daily for patients> 3 years, targeting trough concentrations of 5–15 ng/ml. The separate SIOP ESCP LGG document contains fuller information on dosing, adverse events, dose modification and supportive care.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.4. Radiotherapy
document_sections.content: Chemotherapy is used to defer or avoid radiotherapy and thereby reduce potential cognitive, endocrine and vascular injury, dependent on site, and radiation-induced malignancy. Patients with panhypopituitarism already have impaired HPA-axis function. Children younger than 5 years appear at greatest risk of conformal-radiotherapy sequelae, including moya-moya, increasing deficits over time for supratentorial midline tumors and the greatest cognitive decline. Neurocognitive decline has also been observed in children with LGG younger than 7 years when tumor location increases dose or exposed volume in the left temporal lobe or hippocampus, even with proton therapy and regardless of NF1. Younger age therefore limits first-line radiotherapy choice; age <10 years has also been identified as a vasculopathy risk factor. Radiotherapy is consequently deferred particularly in young patients. Once the main treatment for incompletely resected pLGG, radiotherapy remains standard salvage therapy or a primary option in selected cases where nearby normal tissue can be optimally spared. High-precision methods, including proton therapy, may reduce long-term toxicity, but prospective comparisons with systemic therapy are needed. A radiotherapy dose between 50.4 and 54 Gy is recommended; a dose under 54 Gy could reduce vasculopathy risk. With multidisciplinary-board agreement, upfront radiotherapy may be considered if even minimal growth threatens substantial morbidity or radiotherapy-related neurocognitive risk is low. Craniospinal irradiation may be an option for disseminated disease after chemotherapy failure. Radiotherapy should be avoided as far as possible in children with NF1 because their risks of second malignancy and late vascular effects are higher. Older patients with unresectable diffuse astrocytoma or midbrain/thalamic tumors may have suboptimal long-term survival and might benefit from early radiotherapy.

document_sections.content: Table 2 presents proposed evaluations at diagnosis, during therapy and at its completion.

document_sections.content: The table outlines the timing of physical and anthropometric examinations, neurological examination, blood and biochemical tests, brain and selected spine MRI, ophthalmology, GFR, selected audiometry, endocrinology and neurocognitive assessment. It notes that a course depends on the regimen; MRI at week 12 may be considered for infants and patients with threatened vision. Scheduled ophthalmology applies when the optic pathway is involved, or sooner when clinically indicated. Audiometry methods depend on whether the child is over or under three years; endocrine assessment applies to chiasmatic-hypothalamic tumors, and the marked GFR and audiometry assessments apply to platinum-based regimens.

document_sections.heading: 7. Concomitant medications
document_sections.content: Children with CHG may need thyroid hormone, hydrocortisone, growth hormone or anti-diuretic hormone replacement, or treatment for precocious puberty. Hormone therapy can continue without adjustment during chemotherapy, but whether to stop growth hormone replacement depends on institutional guidance because evidence is inconclusive. In a retrospective study of 124 patients with midline pLGG, growth hormonal replacement therapy (GHRT) was not associated with a statistically significant increase in relapse risk compared with no GHRT; prospective safety evidence is still needed. Antiepileptic medication generally continues when indicated, while possible interactions with antiepileptic and supportive-care drugs should be checked. The separate SIOP ESCP LGG document addresses particular chemotherapy interactions.

document_sections.heading: 8. Patient follow-up
document_sections.content: Surveillance depends on age, NF1, primary tumor site, extent of resection, integrated pathology, treatment type, relapse history and time since diagnosis. Late relapse can occur, although rarely. Krishnatry et al. associated radiotherapy with later deaths from any cause and from tumor in 1202 adult survivors of childhood pLGG. Zaazoue et al. proposed less frequent imaging after gross total resection; for such patients, imaging less often than the Table 3 schedule after the 5th year can be considered.

document_sections.content: The table proposes follow-up examinations and imaging across treatment groups and describes additional audiological, renal and endocrine surveillance for observation, chemotherapy and radiotherapy groups. Ophthalmological follow-up is mandatory for OPG. Neurocognitive testing should account for tumor site and treatment; it could be omitted for an untreated spinal tumor.

document_sections.heading: 9. Conclusion
document_sections.content: Despite generally favorable prognosis, pLGG comprises varied tumors that often follow a chronic course. Developments in molecular pathology and targeted therapies are expected to change treatment rapidly. Meanwhile, decisions are advised to be multidisciplinary and to weigh resectability alongside maximal preservation of neurological, visual and endocrine function and limitation of complications.
